scenario.setting: Post-incident review, 15 minutes after a system outage was resolved
scenario.brief: A website went down for 20 minutes. The immediate cause was a server running out of memory. Your team lead wants the real root cause before everyone moves on, not just 'the server ran out of memory.'
scenario.context: The 5-Whys technique asks 'why' repeatedly until you reach a genuinely actionable root cause, not just the first, most obvious symptom.

steps.title: Running the 5-Whys
steps.prompt: Given: 'The server ran out of memory' → Why? 'A memory leak in the new caching module.' → Why? 'The caching module doesn't release memory for expired cache entries.' → Why? 'This code path was never tested with long-running processes.' Write what you think the 4th 'why' and root-cause finding should be (2-3 sentences).
steps.modelAnswer: Why wasn't this code path tested with long-running processes? Because the team's testing process only runs short-duration test suites (a few minutes), and no test scenario simulates the days-long uptime a production server actually experiences. Root cause: the testing process itself has a structural gap — it doesn't include long-running scenario tests — which is why a memory leak like this can pass all existing tests and still cause a production outage.
steps.reasoning: The real root cause in a 5-Whys chain is usually a process or systemic gap (like missing long-running tests here), not a single line of buggy code — the buggy code is a symptom of the process gap that allowed it to go undetected.
steps.tip: Keep asking 'why' past the first technical-sounding answer (the memory leak) — a technical bug is rarely the true root cause on its own; there's almost always a process reason the bug wasn't caught before production.
steps.mistake: Stopping at 'a memory leak caused it' and fixing only that specific leak addresses this one incident but leaves the testing process gap in place, meaning a different long-running bug could cause the same kind of outage again.
steps.recommendation: Propose a specific process fix as your root-cause action (add long-running test scenarios), not just a code fix (patch this specific leak) — the process fix is what actually prevents the next similar incident.

steps.title: Choosing the Right Fix
steps.prompt: Given the process-gap root cause found, what should the post-incident action items focus on?
options: Only patching this specific memory leak
Patching this leak AND adding long-running test scenarios to the testing process, addressing both the immediate bug and the systemic gap that let it through
Firing whoever wrote the caching module
Doing nothing since the immediate issue is now resolved
steps.reasoning: A complete post-incident action set addresses both the immediate technical fix (patch the leak) and the systemic process gap (add long-running tests) — fixing only one of the two either leaves the current outage's cause unpatched, or leaves the door open for the next similar bug to slip through the same testing gap.
steps.tip: Always pair an immediate technical fix with a process-level action item when a 5-Whys chain reveals a systemic gap — the immediate fix resolves this incident, the process fix prevents the next one.
steps.mistake: Patching only the specific leak without addressing the testing gap is a common but incomplete response — it treats this incident as isolated rather than as a symptom of a process weakness likely to produce similar incidents again.
steps.recommendation: Assign a specific owner and timeline to the process-level action item (adding long-running tests), not just the immediate code fix — process improvements are the ones most likely to be deprioritized once the immediate fire is out.

outcome.reflectionPrompt: Think of a recurring problem you've experienced (personal or team). If you ran a 5-Whys on it, what do you think the real root cause would turn out to be?
